# Overview



CSUBST (/si:sʌbst/) is a sophisticated computational toolkit designed for analyzing **C**ombinatorial **SUBST**itutions in codon sequences across phylogenetic trees. At its core, csubst addresses a fundamental question in molecular evolution: how do protein-coding sequences evolve independently across different lineages to arrive at similar amino acid states? This tool enables researchers to detect, quantify, and visualize molecular convergence—the phenomenon where unrelated species evolve similar traits or genetic changes in response to similar selective pressures.

![csubst logo](https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst/blob/master/logo/logo_csubst_large.png?raw=true)

A combinatorial substitution is defined as recurrent substitutions that occur at the same protein site across multiple independent branches of a phylogenetic tree. When multiple substitutions result in the same amino acid, csubst identifies them as convergent amino acid substitutions—a powerful signal of adaptive evolution or functional constraint operating across distantly related species.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13), [setup.py](setup.py#L1-L47)

## Key Features

CSUBST provides a comprehensive suite of analytical capabilities that distinguish it from other molecular evolution tools. The toolkit's architecture is built around four foundational pillars:

**Error-Corrected Convergence Detection**: csubst computes error-corrected rates of protein convergence using null expectations derived from empirical or mechanistic codon substitution models. An experimental approach employs urn sampling from site-wise substitution frequencies to establish robust baseline expectations, helping distinguish true convergent signals from stochastic processes.

**Flexible Foreground Lineage Specification**: Users can define "foreground" lineages—branches of particular interest for convergence analysis—through flexible pattern matching. The toolkit enables comparison between foreground lineages and their neighboring branches, facilitating tests of whether convergent evolution is enriched in specific evolutionary contexts.

**Higher-Order Convergence Detection**: Beyond pairwise comparisons, csubst implements heuristic algorithms to detect higher-order convergence involving more than two branches simultaneously. This capability is crucial for understanding complex evolutionary scenarios where similar amino acid changes occur across multiple independent lineages.

**Integrated Structural Mapping**: Convergent substitutions can be mapped onto three-dimensional protein structures, enabling researchers to explore the spatial distribution of convergent changes and investigate whether they cluster in functional domains or active sites.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L6-L16), [csubst](csubst#L1-L349), [main_site.py](csubst/main_site.py#L1-L720)

## Architecture Overview

The csubst toolkit follows a modular design pattern that separates input processing, statistical computation, and visualization into distinct functional components. This architecture enables efficient parallel processing and flexible workflow customization for different analytical scenarios.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        A[FASTA Alignment] --> E[Parser]
        B[Newick Tree] --> E[Parser]
        C[Foreground Specification] --> E[Parser]
    end
    
    subgraph Processing["Processing Layer"]
        E --> F[IQ-TREE Integration]
        F --> G[Ancestral State Reconstruction]
        G --> H[Substitution Tensor]
        H --> I[Branch Combination Search]
    end
    
    subgraph Analysis["Analysis Layer"]
        I --> J[Convergence Rate Calculation]
        I --> K[Omega dN/dS Estimation]
        I --> L[Error-Correction & Null Models]
        I --> M[Higher-Order Detection]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Layer"]
        J --> N[Statistical Tables]
        K --> N
        L --> N
        M --> N
        N --> O[Structure Mapping]
        N --> P[Visualization]
    end
    
    style Input fill:#e1f5ff
    style Processing fill:#fff4e1
    style Analysis fill:#e8f5e9
    style Output fill:#f3e5f5
```

The processing pipeline begins with parsing input files, followed by ancestral state reconstruction using IQ-TREE. CSUBST then constructs multi-dimensional substitution tensors that encode all observed and inferred changes across the tree. These tensors serve as the foundation for branch combination searches, statistical hypothesis testing, and ultimately the identification of significant convergent evolution patterns.

Sources: [main_analyze.py](csubst/main_analyze.py#L20-L288), [substitution.py](csubst/substitution.py#L12-L369), [combination.py](csubst/combination.py#L13-L331)

## Command-Line Interface

CSUBST operates through four primary subcommands, each designed for specific analytical tasks. The toolkit's CLI is built using Python's argparse framework, providing consistent argument handling and comprehensive help documentation.

![csubst workflow](https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst/blob/master/logo/method.png?raw=true)

| Subcommand | Purpose | Key Inputs | Primary Outputs |
|------------|---------|------------|-----------------|
| `csubst dataset` | Generates test datasets for learning and validation | Dataset name (PGK/PEPC) | Sample alignment, tree, foreground file |
| `csubst analyze` | Core convergence analysis and statistical testing | Alignment, tree, foreground file | Branch combinations, convergence rates, ω<sub>C</sub> |
| `csubst simulate` | Generates synthetic datasets under convergent scenarios | Alignment, tree, evolutionary parameters | Simulated alignments for validation |
| `csubst site` | Site-wise analysis and structural mapping | Alignment, tree, branch IDs | Per-site substitution patterns, structure files |

The `analyze` subcommand is the heart of csubst, performing the full analytical workflow from ancestral state reconstruction through statistical testing. Users can customize the analysis through numerous parameters controlling codon models, branch selection criteria, and statistical thresholds. The `site` command extends this analysis by providing detailed per-site information and generating files for visualization in molecular graphics programs like PyMOL or Chimera.

Sources: [csubst](csubst#L1-L349), [main_dataset.py](csubst/main_dataset.py#L1-L13), [README.md](README.md#L38-L68)

## Core Components

The csubst implementation leverages several key Python modules that work together to deliver comprehensive convergence analysis capabilities.

**Combination Analysis** ([combination.py](csubst/combination.py#L1-L331)): This module implements the core algorithms for identifying and evaluating branch combinations. It includes functions for enumerating node combinations, calculating substitution patterns across branches, and managing dependency relationships between foreground lineages. The module supports both exhaustive searches of all possible combinations and efficient sampling strategies for large trees.

**Substitution Processing** ([substitution.py](csubst/substitution.py#L1-L369)): Handles the construction and manipulation of substitution tensors—multi-dimensional arrays that encode substitution events across branches, sites, and codon states. The module includes optimized Cython implementations ([substitution_cy.pyx](csubst/substitution_cy.pyx)) for performance-critical operations, enabling analysis of large phylogenomic datasets.

**Omega Calculation** ([omega.py](csubst/omega.py#L1-L362)): Implements the computation of ω (dN/dS) values for branch combinations, distinguishing between convergent (ω<sub>C</sub>) and non-convergent evolution. The module provides error-corrected estimates and supports various statistical transformations for hypothesis testing.

**Foreground Management** ([foreground.py](csubst/foreground.py#L1-L582)): Manages the specification and analysis of foreground lineages, including flexible pattern matching, randomization procedures for statistical testing, and clade permutation methods. This module enables researchers to test whether convergence is enriched in specific evolutionary contexts.

**Tree Operations** ([tree.py](csubst/tree.py#L1-L379)): Provides utilities for tree manipulation, including branch length rescaling, node distance calculations, and visualization support. The module integrates with the ETE3 toolkit for advanced tree visualization capabilities.

Sources: [combination.py](csubst/combination.py#L1-L331), [substitution.py](csubst/substitution.py#L1-L369), [omega.py](csubst/omega.py#L1-L362), [foreground.py](csubst/foreground.py#L1-L582), [tree.py](csubst/tree.py#L1-L379)

## Project Structure

The csubst codebase is organized into logical modules that separate concerns and enable efficient development and maintenance. The project includes both Python source files and Cython extensions for performance optimization.

```
csubst/
├── Core Analysis Modules
│   ├── main_analyze.py      # Primary analysis workflow
│   ├── main_simulate.py     # Simulation framework
│   ├── main_site.py         # Site-wise analysis and mapping
│   ├── main_dataset.py      # Dataset generation utilities
│
├── Statistical Engines
│   ├── combination.py       # Branch combination algorithms
│   ├── substitution.py       # Substitution tensor operations
│   ├── omega.py             # dN/dS calculations
│   └── foreground.py        # Foreground lineage management
│
├── Performance Optimization
│   ├── combination_cy.pyx   # Cython acceleration for combinations
│   ├── substitution_cy.pyx  # Cython acceleration for substitutions
│   ├── omega_cy.pyx         # Cython acceleration for omega
│   └── parallel.py          # Parallel processing utilities
│
├── Input/Output Handling
│   ├── parser_iqtree.py     # IQ-TREE output parsing
│   ├── parser_pymol.py      # PyMOL integration
│   ├── parser_biodb.py      # Bio-database parsing
│   ├── tree.py              # Tree operations
│   ├── sequence.py          # Sequence utilities
│   └── genetic_code.py      # Genetic code tables
│
├── Data Resources
│   ├── dataset/             # Example datasets (PGK, PEPC)
│   └── substitution_matrix/ # ECM codon substitution matrices
│
└── Supporting Utilities
    ├── param.py             # Parameter management
    ├── table.py             # Table operations
    ├── utility.py           # General utilities
    └── __init__.py          # Package initialization
```

The modular structure enables users to extend csubst functionality by adding new analysis modules or modifying existing components. Performance-critical operations are implemented in Cython to provide near-C speed while maintaining Python's ease of use.

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L1-L47), [get_repo_structure](csubst/)

## Getting Started

For developers and researchers new to csubst, the recommended learning path begins with understanding the core concepts and progressively building expertise through hands-on experimentation.

1. **Installation**: Begin with the [Installation](3-installation) guide to set up csubst on your system. The toolkit is available through both conda and pip, with conda recommended for ease of dependency management.

2. **Quick Start**: Follow the [Quick Start](2-quick-start) tutorial to run your first analysis using the included PGK dataset. This provides immediate hands-on experience with the complete workflow.

3. **Basic Usage**: Explore the [Basic Usage](4-basic-usage) guide to understand the essential parameters and workflow for typical convergence analyses.

4. **Core Concepts**: Dive deeper into the theoretical foundations through [Combinatorial Substitutions](5-combinatorial-substitutions), [Foreground Lineages](6-foreground-lineages), and [Codon Substitution Models](7-codon-substitution-models) to understand the statistical and evolutionary principles underlying the analysis.

> [!TIP]
> Start with the `csubst dataset --name PGK` command to generate a small test dataset, then run `csubst analyze` to see the complete workflow in action. This provides immediate feedback and helps validate your installation before moving to your own data.

CSUBST has been applied in published research to detect macroevolutionary genotype-phenotype associations, demonstrating its utility for understanding convergent evolution at the molecular level. The toolkit's error-corrected approach helps distinguish true adaptive convergence from random similarity, providing researchers with confidence in their evolutionary interpretations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L71-L83), [main_dataset.py](csubst/main_dataset.py#L1-L13), [setup.py](setup.py#L1-L47)

# Quick Start



Quick Start provides the fastest path to getting hands-on experience with CSUBST. This guide will walk you through installation, testing the toolkit with provided datasets, and understanding the core workflow for analyzing molecular convergence in coding sequences.

![CSUBST Logo](https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst/blob/master/logo/logo_csubst_large.png?raw=true)

CSUBST (pronounced `/si:sʌbst/`) is a specialized toolkit designed for detecting and analyzing combinatorial substitutions—recurrent amino acid changes occurring at the same protein site across independent evolutionary lineages. The toolkit implements error-corrected statistical methods to distinguish true convergent evolution from random mutations, integrates codon substitution models for ancestral state reconstruction, and supports protein structure mapping for visualizing convergence patterns.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L29)

## Installation

CSUBST runs on Python 3.6 or higher and offers two installation methods depending on your preferred package management workflow.

### Option 1: Conda Installation (Recommended)

The Bioconda channel provides the most streamlined installation experience, automatically handling all dependencies including IQ-TREE:

```bash
conda install bioconda::csubst
```

### Option 2: Pip Installation

For users preferring pip, you'll need to install IQ-TREE separately before proceeding with CSUBST:

```bash
# Install dependencies
pip install numpy cython

# Install CSUBST from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst
```

> [!TIP]
> **Installation Note**: When using pip installation, ensure IQ-TREE is in your system PATH before running CSUBST, as the toolkit relies on it for ancestral state reconstruction and codon model calculations.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L31-L42), [setup.py](/setup.py#L1-L47)

## System Architecture

Understanding CSUBST's architecture helps you navigate its capabilities. The toolkit is organized around four main subcommands that form the complete analysis pipeline:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[CSUBST Entry Point] --> B[dataset<br/>Test Data Generation]
    A --> C[analyze<br/>Convergence Rate Calculation]
    A --> D[site<br/>Site-wise Analysis & Mapping]
    A --> E[simulate<br/>Sequence Evolution Simulation]
    
    C --> F[Input Processing]
    C --> G[IQ-TREE Integration]
    C --> H[Substitution Tensor Computation]
    C --> I[Branch Combination Detection]
    
    D --> J[Protein Structure Integration]
    D --> K[Visualization Export]
    
    E --> L[Biased Model Generation]
    E --> M[Pyvolve Evolution]
    
    subgraph Core Libraries
        F --> N[main_dataset.py]
        G --> O[main_analyze.py]
        J --> P[main_site.py]
        L --> Q[main_simulate.py]
    end
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style F fill:#fff4e1
    style G fill:#fff4e1
    style H fill:#fff4e1
```

The architecture reflects a modular design where each subcommand serves a distinct analytical purpose while sharing common computational infrastructure through Cython-optimized modules for tensor operations and phylogenetic parsing.

Sources: [csubst](/csubst/csubst#L1-L200), [main_analyze.py](/csubst/main_analyze.py#L20-L288), [main_site.py](/csubst/main_site.py#L1-L720)

## Quick Test Run

The fastest way to verify your installation and experience CSUBST's workflow is using the provided test datasets. CSUBST includes two pre-configured datasets:

| Dataset | Gene | Size | Description |
|---------|------|------|-------------|
| **PGK** | Phosphoglycerate kinase | Small | Vertebrate PGK genes, ideal for initial testing |
| **PEPC** | Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase | Large | Plant PEPC genes, suitable for stress-testing |

### Step 1: Generate Test Dataset

Generate the PGK dataset, which includes alignment files, a rooted phylogenetic tree, and a foreground lineage specification file:

```bash
csubst dataset --name PGK
```

This command creates several files in your working directory:
- `PGK.alignment.fa` - In-frame codon alignment in FASTA format
- `PGK.tree.nwk` - Rooted phylogenetic tree in Newick format  
- `PGK.foreground.txt` - Foreground lineage specification (tab-separated)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L44-L45), [main_dataset.py](/csubst/main_dataset.py#L4-L13)

### Step 2: Run Convergence Analysis

Execute the core analysis pipeline on the generated dataset:

```bash
csubst analyze \
  --alignment_file PGK.alignment.fa \
  --rooted_tree_file PGK.tree.nwk \
  --foreground PGK.foreground.txt
```

**What this command does:**
- Reads the codon alignment and rooted tree
- Parses the foreground lineage specification (in this case, labeling specific mammalian species)
- Runs IQ-TREE for ancestral state reconstruction using the default ECMK07+F+R4 codon model
- Computes substitution tensors across all branch combinations
- Identifies branch combinations with significant convergent patterns
- Outputs convergence metrics including ω_C (convergence dN/dS), dN_C, and dS_C

**Expected outputs:**
- `csubst_cb_2.tsv` - Branch combination results with convergence statistics
- `csubst_summary.txt` - Analysis summary with key findings
- `PGK.treefile.iqtree` - IQ-TREE tree output
- `PGK.state.iqtree` - Ancestral state reconstructions
- `PGK.rate.iqtree` - Site-specific evolutionary rates

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L47-L51), [main_analyze.py](/csubst/main_analyze.py#L127-L288), [csubst/csubst](/csubst/csubst#L100-L200)

### Understanding the Foreground Specification

The `PGK.foreground.txt` file demonstrates how to specify lineages of interest:

| Lineage ID | Regex Pattern | Interpretation |
|------------|---------------|----------------|
| 1 | Monodelphis_domestica_ENSMODG00000023385 | Opossum (outgroup reference) |
| 2 | Homo_sapiens_ENSG00000170950 | Human |
| 2 | Macaca_mulatta_ENSMMUG00000011998 | Rhesus macaque |
| 2 | Mus_musculus_ENSMUSG00000031233 | Mouse |
| 2 | Rattus_norvegicus_ENSRNOG00000013600 | Rat |

This two-column format uses tab separation where the first column identifies lineages and the second column uses regex-compatible patterns to match tip labels in the tree.

Sources: [PGK.foreground.txt](/csubst/dataset/PGK.foreground.txt#L1-L10)

## Core Subcommands Overview

CSUBST provides four primary subcommands covering the complete convergence analysis workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Start[Start Analysis] --> dataset{Need Test Data?}
    dataset -->|Yes| Generate[Generate Dataset<br/>csubst dataset]
    dataset -->|No| Analyze[Run Analysis<br/>csubst analyze]
    
    Generate --> Analyze
    
    Analyze --> HasResults["Review Results<br/>csubst_cb_2.tsv"]
    HasResults --> Site["Site-wise Analysis?<br/>csubst site"]
    HasResults --> Simulate["Need Simulation?<br/>csubst simulate"]
    
    Site --> Results[Visualization &<br/>Structure Mapping]
    Simulate --> SimResults[Simulated Alignments<br/>for Validation]
    
    style Start fill:#e1f5ff
    style Results fill:#e8f5e9
    style SimResults fill:#e8f5e9
```

### Dataset Generation Command

The `dataset` subcommand creates ready-to-use test datasets:

```bash
csubst dataset --name <dataset_name>
```

**Parameters:**
- `--name`: Dataset name (choices: `PGK`, `PEPC`)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L54-L56)

### Analyze Command

The `analyze` subcommand performs the core convergence analysis:

```bash
csubst analyze \
  --alignment_file <path> \
  --rooted_tree_file <path> \
  --genetic_code <table_id> \
  --iqtree_model <model> \
  --threads <num_cpus> \
  --foreground <path> \
```

**Essential Parameters:**

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--alignment_file` | PATH | Required | In-frame codon alignment (FASTA) |
| `--rooted_tree_file` | PATH | Required | Rooted phylogenetic tree (Newick) |
| `--genetic_code` | INTEGER | 1 | NCBI codon table ID (1 = Standard) |
| `--iqtree_model` | STRING | ECMK07+F+R4 | Codon substitution model for IQ-TREE |
| `--threads` | INTEGER | 1 | Number of CPUs for parallel processing |
| `--foreground` | PATH | None | Foreground lineage specification file |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L58-L68), [csubst/csubst](/csubst/csubst#L60-L75)

### Site Command

The `site` subcommand performs detailed site-wise analysis with protein structure integration:

```bash
csubst site \
  --alignment_file <path> \
  --rooted_tree_file <path> \
  --branch_id <branch_list> \
  --cb_file <csubst_cb_tsv> \
  --untrimmed_cds <cds_fasta> \
  --pdb <pdb_file> \
```

This command requires first running `csubst analyze` to generate the branch combination file (`csubst_cb_2.tsv`). You then specify which branch combinations to analyze in detail, optionally mapping results onto protein 3D structures using PDB files.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L70-L76), [main_site.py](/csubst/main_site.py#L635-L720)

### Simulate Command

The `simulate` subcommand generates synthetic sequences under controlled convergent evolution scenarios:

```bash
csubst simulate \
  --alignment_file <path> \
  --rooted_tree_file <path> \
  --background_omega <value> \
  --foreground_omega <value> \
  --convergent_amino_acids <list> \
  --percent_biased_sub <percentage>
```

**Key Simulation Parameters:**

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--background_omega` | FLOAT | 0.2 | dN/dS for background evolution |
| `--foreground_omega` | FLOAT | 0.2 | dN/dS for foreground lineages |
| `--convergent_amino_acids` | STRING | random1 | Target amino acids (e.g., AQTS, or randomN) |
| `--percent_biased_sub` | FLOAT | 90 | Percentage of biased substitutions in foreground |
| `--percent_convergent_site` | FLOAT | 100 | Percentage of sites evolving convergently |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L78-L86), [main_simulate.py](/csubst/main_simulate.py#L345-L394)

## Verification Checklist

After completing the test run, verify your installation by checking for these outputs:

```
✓ PGK.alignment.fa                (Input alignment file)
✓ PGK.tree.nwk                   (Input tree file)
✓ PGK.foreground.txt             (Foreground specification)
✓ csubst_cb_2.tsv                (Branch combination results)
✓ csubst_summary.txt             (Analysis summary)
✓ PGK.treefile.iqtree            (IQ-TREE tree output)
✓ PGK.state.iqtree               (Ancestral states)
✓ PGK.rate.iqtree                (Rate categories)
```

> [!TIP]
> **Tip**: The `csubst_cb_2.tsv` file contains the primary analytical results. Open it in a spreadsheet or text editor to inspect branch combinations, convergence statistics, and significance values for your test dataset.

# Installation



This guide covers the installation process for CSUBST, a toolkit for detecting molecular convergence in coding sequences. CSUBST requires Python 3.6 or higher and includes **Cython-optimized computational modules** for efficient tensor calculations on phylogenetic trees. The installation process involves setting up both Python dependencies and external tools like IQ-TREE for ancestral state reconstruction.

![CSUBST Logo](https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst/blob/master/logo/logo_csubst_large.png?raw=true)

## System Requirements

CSUBST is designed to run on **Python 3.6 or later** and has been tested on macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. The package includes compiled Cython extensions that require a working C compiler during installation. The build system automatically handles platform-specific configurations, such as macOS-specific NumPy include path adjustments.

**Minimum Requirements:**
- Python 3.6.0+ (officially tested version)
- GCC, Clang, or MSVC compiler for Cython compilation
- 4GB RAM minimum (8GB+ recommended for large datasets)
- Multiple CPU cores recommended for parallel computations

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L1-L47), [README.md](README.md#L24-L25)

## Installation Methods

CSUBST offers two primary installation approaches. The **conda method** is strongly recommended for beginners as it automatically handles all dependencies including IQ-TREE. The pip method provides flexibility for advanced users who need specific version control.

### Option 1: Conda Installation (Recommended)

The conda installation via Bioconda is the most straightforward approach, automatically managing all dependencies including the critical IQ-TREE executable:

```bash
conda install bioconda::csubst
```

This single command installs CSUBST along with all required Python packages (ete3, numpy, scipy, pandas, joblib, cython, matplotlib, threadpoolctl) and IQ-TREE for phylogenetic analysis. The Bioconda channel ensures version compatibility and simplifies environment management.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L27-L30), [setup.py](setup.py#L30)

### Option 2: pip Installation

For pip installation, you must manually install prerequisites before installing CSUBST. This two-step process ensures proper compilation of Cython extensions:

```bash
# Step 1: Install IQ-TREE separately
# Download from: https://iqtree.github.io/

# Step 2: Install NumPy and Cython first (critical requirement)
pip install numpy cython

# Step 3: Install CSUBST from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst
```

> [!TIP]
> **Critical**: NumPy and Cython must be installed **before** CSUBST installation because the setup.py script imports NumPy's C headers during the Cython extension compilation process. Installing them afterward will cause build failures.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L37), [setup.py#L9-L10](setup.py#L9-L10)

## Installation Architecture

The CSUBST installation process involves several components working together to create a functional analysis environment:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Installation Start] --> B{Installation Method}
    
    B -->|Conda| C["Single Command<br/>conda install bioconda::csubst"]
    B -->|pip| D[Multi-Step Process]
    
    C --> E[Auto-Install Dependencies]
    D --> F[Install IQ-TREE Manually]
    D --> G[Install NumPy & Cython]
    D --> H["pip install csubst"]
    
    E --> I[Cython Compilation]
    F --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I
    
    I --> J[Build Extensions]
    J --> K["substitution_cy.pyx"]
    J --> L["combination_cy.pyx"]
    J --> M["omega_cy.pyx"]
    
    K --> N[Install CLI Script]
    L --> N
    M --> N
    
    N --> O["Verification<br/>csubst -h"]
    
    style C fill:#90EE90
    style E fill:#90EE90
    style I fill:#FFD700
    style N fill:#87CEEB
```

## Dependency Breakdown

CSUBST requires a comprehensive set of Python packages and external tools. The table below provides detailed information about each dependency:

| Dependency | Category | Version Requirement | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|-------------------|---------|
| **Python** | Runtime | ≥3.6.0 | Core execution environment |
| **ete3** | Phylogenetics | Latest | Tree manipulation and analysis |
| **numpy** | Computation | Latest | Numerical operations and tensor storage |
| **scipy** | Scientific | Latest | Statistical functions |
| **pandas** | Data I/O | Latest | DataFrame operations and CSV/TSV handling |
| **joblib** | Parallelization | Latest | Multi-CPU processing |
| **matplotlib** | Visualization | Latest | Plotting and chart generation |
| **threadpoolctl** | Performance | Latest | Thread pool management |
| **cython** | Compilation | Latest | Python-to-C compilation |
| **setuptools** | Build | ≥18.0 | Package installation framework |
| **IQ-TREE** | External Tool | Latest | Ancestral state reconstruction |

> [!TIP]
> **Build Tools**: A C compiler (GCC on Linux, Clang on macOS, MSVC on Windows) is required for Cython compilation. Conda environments typically include necessary compilers automatically.

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L30-L32), [csubst/csubst#L80-L99](csubst/csubst#L80-L99)

## Cython Extensions

CSUBST includes three Cython-optimized modules that provide significant performance improvements for computationally intensive operations:

- **substitution_cy.pyx**: Computes combinatorial substitution tensors with NumPy array operations optimized through Cython decorators that disable bounds checking and negative index wrapping for maximum speed
- **combination_cy.pyx**: Handles branch combination detection logic
- **omega_cy.pyx**: Calculates dN/dS ratios (ω) for convergent sites

These extensions are automatically compiled during installation using the `cythonize()` function with NumPy include paths. The compilation process generates platform-specific shared libraries (.so files on Unix, .pyd files on Windows) that are loaded transparently when CSUBST runs.

Sources: [setup.py#L33-L37](setup.py#L33-L37), [csubst/substitution_cy.pyx#L7-L9](csubst/substitution_cy.pyx#L7-L9)

## Installation Verification

After installation, verify that CSUBST is correctly installed by checking the version and available commands:

```bash
# Check installation
csubst --version

# List available subcommands
csubst -h
```

Expected output should show version information (e.g., "CSUBST version: 1.4.20") and available subcommands including `analyze`, `dataset`, `site`, and `simulate`.

Sources: [csubst/__init__.py](csubst/__init__.py#L1), [csubst/csubst#L57-L59](csubst/csubst#L57-L59)

## Package Data Installation

CSUBST includes essential data files that are automatically installed with the package:

- **substitution_matrix/** directory: Contains ECMrest.dat and ECMunrest.dat substitution matrices for empirical codon models
- **dataset/** directory: Includes example datasets (PGK, PEPC) for testing and tutorials

These files are specified in the `package_data` section of setup.py and are installed to the Python site-packages directory, making them accessible to CSUBST commands via relative imports.

Sources: [setup.py#L41-L44](setup.py#L41-L44), [get_repo_structure](csubst/substitution_matrix)

## CLI Script Installation

The installation creates a command-line interface script named `csubst` that provides access to all analysis functions:

```bash
# The installed script location
csubst/csubst  →  /path/to/python/bin/csubst
```

This script serves as the main entry point and provides four primary subcommands:
- `csubst analyze`: Main convergence analysis pipeline
- `csubst dataset`: Generate test datasets
- `csubst site`: Site-wise substitution mapping
- `csubst simulate`: Simulate convergent evolution

Sources: [setup.py#L31](setup.py#L31), [csubst/csubst#L11-L49](csubst/csubst#L11-L49)

## Troubleshooting

### Common Installation Issues

**Problem**: `fatal error: numpy/arrayobject.h file not found`

**Solution**: Ensure NumPy is installed **before** CSUBST installation. On macOS, the setup.py script includes automatic environment variable handling for this issue, but manual installation order is still critical.

**Problem**: IQ-TREE not found after pip installation

**Solution**: When using pip, IQ-TREE must be installed separately. Download from https://iqtree.github.io/ and ensure the executable is in your system PATH. You can also specify the IQ-TREE path using the `--iqtree_exe` parameter during analysis.

**Problem**: Cython compilation failures

**Solution**: Verify you have a working C compiler. On Ubuntu: `sudo apt-get install build-essential`. On macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`). The setup.py script includes platform-specific handling for macOS to ensure proper NumPy header inclusion.

Sources: [setup.py#L11-L13](setup.py#L11-L13), [csubst/csubst#L81-L82](csubst/csubst#L81-L82)

# Basic Usage



This guide provides a practical introduction to running csubst for molecular convergence detection. You'll learn how to prepare your data, execute analyses, and interpret the results through CSUBST's four primary subcommands. CSUBST analyzes combinatorial substitutions—recurrent substitutions at the same protein site across multiple independent phylogenetic branches—using error-corrected statistical methods that account for neutral substitution expectations.

![CSUBST Method Overview](https://github.com/kfuku52/csubst/blob/master/logo/method.png?raw=true)

## Command Architecture

CSUBST follows a modular command-line interface design with four main subcommands that address different aspects of convergence analysis. The architecture enables flexible workflows ranging from quick test runs to comprehensive evolutionary studies.

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[CSUBST CLI] --> B[dataset]
    A --> C[analyze]
    A --> D[site]
    A --> E[simulate]
    
    B --> B1["Generate Test Datasets<br/>PGK or PEPC"]
    
    C --> C1["Calculate Convergence Rates<br/>ωC, dNc, dSc"]
    C --> C2["Branch Combinations<br/>K=2 to K=N"]
    C --> C3["Statistical Testing<br/>Null expectations"]
    
    D --> D1["Site-wise Analysis<br/>Specific branch combinations"]
    D --> D2["Structural Mapping<br/>PDB/AlphaFold integration"]
    
    E --> E1["Simulated Evolution<br/>Convergent scenarios"]
    E --> E2["Biased Substitutions<br/>Controlled convergence intensity"]
    
    C --> D
    C --> F["Output Files<br/>TSV tables + plots"]
    D --> F
    E --> F
```

Sources: [csubst](csubst/csubst#L1-L100), [README.md](README.md#L35-L50)

## Subcommand Overview

Each CSUBST subcommand serves a distinct purpose in the analysis pipeline, from data preparation to detailed investigation and simulation.

| Subcommand | Primary Function | Key Outputs | Typical Use Case |
|------------|------------------|-------------|------------------|
| **dataset** | Generate ready-to-use test datasets | alignment.fa, tree.nwk, foreground.txt | Quick testing, learning the workflow |
| **analyze** | Detect combinatorial substitutions across branch combinations | csubst_cb_*.tsv (convergence statistics), csubst_b.tsv (branches), csubst_s.tsv (sites) | Main convergence detection analysis |
| **site** | Characterize site-wise substitutions on specific branches and map to structures | Visualization plots, structure files, csubst_site.tsv | Detailed investigation of convergent sites |
| **simulate** | Generate synthetic alignments under controlled convergent evolution | Simulated alignments, control datasets | Method validation, power analysis |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L50), [csubst](csubst/csubst#L100-L250)

## Project Structure

The CSUBST package organizes its functionality across multiple specialized modules, with the main entry point providing unified access to all analytical workflows.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[csubst/] --> B[Core Analysis Modules]
    A --> C[Data Processing]
    A --> D[Visualization]
    A --> E[Datasets & Resources]
    
    B --> B1[main_analyze.py<br/>Convergence detection]
    B --> B2[main_site.py<br/>Site-wise analysis]
    B --> B3[main_simulate.py<br/>Sequence simulation]
    B --> B4[main_dataset.py<br/>Dataset generation]
    
    C --> C1[tree.py<br/>Tree parsing]
    C --> C2[sequence.py<br/>Sequence handling]
    C --> C3[foreground.py<br/>Lineage annotation]
    
    D --> D1[parser_pymol.py<br/>Structure mapping]
    D --> D2[parser_iqtree.py<br/>ASR integration]
    
    E --> E1[dataset/<br/>Test alignments]
    E --> E2[substitution_matrix/<br/>Codon models]
```

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L29-L44), [get_repo_structure](csubst)

## Quick Start Workflow

Get started immediately with CSUBST's built-in test datasets. This complete workflow demonstrates the typical analysis pipeline from data preparation through convergence detection.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Generate Test Dataset] --> B[Run Convergence Analysis]
    B --> C[Examine Results]
    C --> D[Optional: Site Analysis]
    D --> E[Optional: Structural Mapping]
    
    A --> A1["csubst dataset --name PGK"]
    B --> B1["csubst analyze<br/>--alignment_file alignment.fa<br/>--rooted_tree_file tree.nwk<br/>--foreground foreground.txt"]
    C --> C1["View csubst_cb_stats.tsv<br/>Identify top convergent pairs"]
    D --> D1["csubst site --branch_id fg<br/>--cb_file csubst_cb_2.tsv"]
    E --> E1["--pdb 3SV0 or besthit"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L40), [main_dataset.py](csubst/main_dataset.py#L4-L13)

### Step 1: Generate Test Dataset

CSUBST includes curated test datasets to help you understand the analysis workflow without needing to prepare your own data. The **PGK** dataset (vertebrate phosphoglycerate kinase genes) provides a smaller, faster-running example, while **PEPC** (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase genes) offers a more complex scenario with multiple foreground lineage categories.

```bash
# Generate the PGK test dataset
csubst dataset --name PGK
```

This command copies the following files to your current directory:

- **PGK.alignment.fa** → `alignment.fa`: In-frame codon alignment in FASTA format
- **PGK.tree.nwk** → `tree.nwk`: Rooted phylogenetic tree in Newick format
- **PGK.foreground.txt** → `foreground.txt`: Foreground lineage specification file

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L35-L40), [main_dataset.py](csubst/main_dataset.py#L4-L13)

### Step 2: Run Convergence Analysis

The `analyze` subcommand performs the core convergence detection analysis. This step reconstructs ancestral states using IQ-TREE, computes substitution tensors, and searches for combinatorial substitutions across branch combinations.

```bash
csubst analyze \
  --alignment_file alignment.fa \
  --rooted_tree_file tree.nwk \
  --foreground foreground.txt \
  --threads 4 \
  --iqtree_model ECMK07+F+R4 \
  --genetic_code 1
```

> [!TIP]
> Ensure that IQ-TREE is installed and accessible in your system PATH. If you installed CSUBST via conda, IQ-TREE is typically included as a dependency.

Key parameters for this command:
- **--alignment_file**: Path to your codon alignment (in-frame coding sequences)
- **--rooted_tree_file**: Path to your rooted phylogenetic tree
- **--foreground**: Optional file specifying foreground lineages of interest
- **--threads**: Number of CPU cores to use for parallel computation (default: 1)
- **--iqtree_model**: Codon substitution model for ancestral state reconstruction (default: ECMK07+F+R4)
- **--genetic_code**: NCBI codon table ID (default: 1 for standard genetic code)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L55), [csubst](csubst/csubst#L44-L60), [main_analyze.py](csubst/main_analyze.py#L127-L288)

### Step 3: Examine Results

The analysis generates multiple output files containing convergence statistics at different levels of resolution.

**Primary output files:**
- **csubst_cb_stats.tsv**: Summary statistics for each branch combination, including ωC (omega C), dNc, and dSc
- **csubst_cb_2.tsv**: Detailed branch combination statistics for K=2 (branch pairs)
- **csubst_b.tsv**: Branch-wise substitution statistics
- **csubst_s.tsv**: Site-wise substitution statistics (if `--s yes`)

For the PGK dataset, the csubst_cb_stats.tsv file will rank branch combinations by their convergence statistics, allowing you to identify which pairs show the strongest evidence for convergent evolution.

Sources: [main_analyze.py](csubst/main_analyze.py#L250-L288), [README.md](README.md#L50-L55)

### Step 4: Site-wise Analysis (Optional)

Once you've identified interesting branch combinations, use the `site` subcommand to perform detailed site-wise analysis and optionally map substitutions onto protein structures.

```bash
# Analyze all foreground branch pairs
csubst site \
  --alignment_file alignment.fa \
  --rooted_tree_file tree.nwk \
  --branch_id fg \
  --cb_file csubst_cb_2.tsv
```

The `--branch_id` parameter accepts either:
- **fg**: Analyze all foreground branch pairs
- **INT,INT,INT,...**: Specific branch IDs (comma-separated)

Sources: [csubst](csubst/csubst#L182-L200), [main_site.py](csubst/main_site.py#L635-L720)

### Step 5: Structural Mapping (Optional)

CSUBST can map convergent substitutions onto 3D protein structures from PDB, AlphaFold, or AlphaFill databases.

```bash
csubst site \
  --alignment_file alignment.fa \
  --rooted_tree_file tree.nwk \
  --branch_id fg \
  --cb_file csubst_cb_2.tsv \
  --pdb besthit \
  --database pdb,alphafill,alphafold
```

This option will:
1. Search structure databases using your sequence
2. Align the sequence to the best-matching structure
3. Generate PyMOL sessions and rendered images
4. Color-code residues based on convergence probabilities

Sources: [csubst](csubst/csubst#L200-L250), [parser_pymol.py](csubst/parser_pymol.py)

## Foreground Lineage Specification

The foreground file allows you to specify lineages of particular interest for targeted convergence analysis. This is particularly useful when you have a priori hypotheses about which branches might be experiencing convergent evolution.

### Format

The foreground file is a tab-delimited text file with two columns:
1. **Lineage ID**: A unique identifier for each lineage (integer or string)
2. **Regex pattern**: Regular expression matching tip labels belonging to that lineage

### Example: PGK Foreground File

```
1	Monodelphis_domestica_ENSMODG00000023385
2	Homo_sapiens_ENSG00000170950
2	Macaca_mulatta_ENSMMUG00000011998
2	Callithrix_jacchus_ENSCJAG00000022394
2	Mus_musculus_ENSMUSG00000031233
2	Rattus_norvegicus_ENSRNOG00000013600
2	Oryctolagus_cuniculus_ENSOCUG00000005270
2	Ovis_aries_ENSOARG00000008736
2	Sus_scrofa_ENSSSCG00000001738
```

In this example:
- Lineage 1: Outgroup species (Monodelphis domestica - opossum)
- Lineage 2: Multiple placental mammal species for comparison

The regex pattern matches exact species names, but you can use more complex patterns (e.g., `.*_ENS.*` to match all species with Ensembl identifiers).

Sources: [foreground.py](csubst/foreground.py#L240-L260), [dataset/PGK.foreground.txt](csubst/dataset/PGK.foreground.txt#L1-L10)

### Example: PEPC Foreground File (Multi-category)

The PEPC dataset demonstrates how to specify multiple foreground categories:

```
name	C4	C4_monocot	C4_dicot	crop
Alternanthera_pungens_.*	1	0	1	0
Amaranthus_hypochondriacus_.*	1	0	1	1
Cyperus_sanguinolentus_.*	1	1	0	0
Eleocharis_vivipara_.*	1	1	0	0
```

This multi-column format allows you to analyze convergence with respect to different traits simultaneously (e.g., C4 photosynthesis, monocot vs. dicot classification, crop status).

Sources: [dataset/PEPC.foreground.tsv](csubst/dataset/PEPC.foreground.tsv#L1-L20)

## Common Parameters Reference

This section provides a comprehensive reference for the most commonly used parameters across CSUBST subcommands.

### Essential Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description | Applies To |
|-----------|---------|-------------|------------|
| `--alignment_file` | Required | PATH to in-frame codon alignment (FASTA) | analyze, site, simulate |
| `--rooted_tree_file` | Required | PATH to rooted tree (Newick format) | analyze, site, simulate |
| `--genetic_code` | 1 | NCBI codon table ID (1 = Standard) | analyze, site, simulate |
| `--threads` | 1 | Number of CPUs for parallel computation | analyze, site, simulate |
| `--iqtree_model` | ECMK07+F+R4 | Codon substitution model for ASR | analyze, site, simulate |
| `--foreground` | None | Foreground lineage specification file | analyze, simulate |

### IQ-TREE Related Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `--iqtree_exe` | iqtree | PATH to IQ-TREE executable |
| `--iqtree_model` | ECMK07+F+R4 | Substitution model (MG, GY, ECMK07, ECMrest supported) |
| `--iqtree_redo` | no | Rerun IQ-TREE even if intermediate files exist |

### Analyze-Specific Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `--max_arity` | 2 | Maximum number of branches in combinations (K) |
| `--exhaustive_until` | 2 | Search all combinations until this arity |
| `--max_combination` | 10000 | Max combinations to generate at K+1 |
| `--exclude_sister_pair` | yes | Exclude sister branch combinations |
| `--omegaC_method` | submodel | Method for omega_C calculation (submodel/modelfree) |

Sources: [csubst](csubst/csubst#L44-L250), [README.md](README.md#L40-L60)

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing larger datasets (hundreds of species), use `--exhaustive_until 1` with a foreground file to limit the search space and avoid combinatorial explosion.

## Simulation and Validation

The `simulate` subcommand enables you to generate synthetic sequence alignments under controlled convergent evolutionary scenarios, which is valuable for method validation and power analysis.

```bash
csubst simulate \
  --alignment_file alignment.fa \
  --rooted_tree_file tree.nwk \
  --foreground foreground.txt \
  --background_omega 0.2 \
  --foreground_omega 0.2 \
  --percent_convergent_site 100 \
  --convergent_amino_acids random1 \
  --percent_biased_sub 90
```

Key simulation parameters:
- **--background_omega**: dN/dS for background branches (default: 0.2)
- **--foreground_omega**: dN/dS for foreground branches (default: 0.2)
- **--percent_convergent_site**: Percentage of sites evolving convergently (default: 100)
- **--convergent_amino_acids**: Target amino acids (e.g., AQTS or randomN)
- **--percent_biased_sub**: Percentage of substitutions biased toward convergent amino acids (default: 90)

Sources: [main_simulate.py](csubst/main_simulate.py#L345-L394), [csubst](csubst/csubst#L150-L180)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Issue | Possible Cause | Solution |
|-------|----------------|----------|
| **IQ-TREE not found** | IQ-TREE not installed or not in PATH | Install IQ-TREE or provide path with `--iqtree_exe` |
| **Alignment not in-frame** | Sequence length not divisible by 3 | Verify codon alignment and remove gaps that disrupt reading frame |
| **Tree tip labels mismatch** | Tip names don't match alignment headers | Ensure exact consistency between tree and FASTA labels |
| **Memory error** | Large dataset with limited RAM | Reduce `--threads`, use `--float_type 32` or 64, or analyze subsets |
| **No foreground combinations** | Incompatible foreground specification | Check regex patterns in foreground file match tip labels |
